claim: Orexin A (hypocretin-1) and orexin B (hypocretin-2) are generated from the same precursor protein called prepro-hypocretin (encoded by hypocretin gene).
source: Orexin A (hypocretin-1) and orexin B (hypocretin-2) (de Lecea et al., 1998; Sakurai et al., 1998), generated from the same precursor protein called prepro-hypocretin (encoded by hypocretin gene), are endogenous ligands for two closely related G-protein-coupled receptors termed orexin-1 receptor (OX1R) and orexin-2 receptor (OX2R) (Sakurai et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to de Lecea et al., 1998 and Sakurai et al., 1998, which are referenced works.

claim: Orexin A and orexin B are endogenous ligands for orexin-1 receptor (OX1R) and orexin-2 receptor (OX2R).
source: Orexin A (hypocretin-1) and orexin B (hypocretin-2) (de Lecea et al., 1998; Sakurai et al., 1998), generated from the same precursor protein called prepro-hypocretin (encoded by hypocretin gene), are endogenous ligands for two closely related G-protein-coupled receptors termed orexin-1 receptor (OX1R) and orexin-2 receptor (OX2R) (Sakurai et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Sakurai et al., 1998.

claim: Knockout of prepro-orexin or dysfunction of OX2R in canines or mice mimics the human sleep disorder narcolepsy.
source: Although orexin was named for its effect on inducing feeding behavior, it gained immense interest in sleep research as the knockout (KO) of prepro-orexin or dysfunction of OX2R in canines or mice reportedly mimics the human sleep disorder narcolepsy (Chemelli et al., 1999; Lin et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chemelli et al., 1999 and Lin et al., 1999.

claim: Narcolepsy is characterized by fragmented sleep/wakefulness, persistent daytime sleepiness and brief episodes of muscle weakness called cataplexy.
source: Narcolepsy is a neurological disorder characterized by fragmented sleep/wakefulness, persistent daytime sleepiness and brief episodes of muscle weakness called cataplexy, which is often triggered by positive emotions.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about narcolepsy that draws from established scientific knowledge.

claim: Cataplexy is often triggered by positive emotions.
source: Narcolepsy is a neurological disorder characterized by fragmented sleep/wakefulness, persistent daytime sleepiness and brief episodes of muscle weakness called cataplexy, which is often triggered by positive emotions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the triggers of cataplexy.

claim: Narcolepsy patients showed a loss of overall hypocretin mRNA, confirming the association between orexin neuronal loss and the pathogenesis of narcolepsy.
source: Narcolepsy patients showed a loss of overall hypocretin mRNA, confirming the association between orexin neuronal loss and the pathogenesis of narcolepsy (Peyron et al., 2000; Thannickal et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Peyron et al., 2000 and Thannickal et al., 2000.

claim: Orexin-producing neurons are exclusively distributed in the lateral hypothalamic area (LHA) and perifornical area.
source: A small number of orexin-producing neurons (orexin neurons) are exclusively distributed in the lateral hypothalamic area (LHA) and perifornical area, but send projections widely throughout the major brain areas (Nambu et al., 1999; Peyron et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Nambu et al., 1999 and Peyron et al., 1998.

claim: Orexin neurons send projections widely throughout the major brain areas.
source: A small number of orexin-producing neurons (orexin neurons) are exclusively distributed in the lateral hypothalamic area (LHA) and perifornical area, but send projections widely throughout the major brain areas (Nambu et al., 1999; Peyron et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Nambu et al., 1999 and Peyron et al., 1998.

claim: Orexin neurons have diverse physiological roles, including the regulation of sleep/wakefulness, energy homeostasis, thermoregulation, and regulation of heart rate and blood pressure.
source: Thus, it is no surprise that orexin neurons have diverse physiological roles, including the regulation of sleep/wakefulness (Chemelli et al., 1999; Lin et al., 1999), energy homeostasis (Yamanaka et al., 2003), thermoregulation (Tupone et al., 2011), as well as regulation of heart rate and blood pressure (Zhang et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published works.

claim: Optogenetic and chemogenetic activation of orexin neurons modulates sleep/wake cycles in rodents.
source: Using optogenetic and/or chemogenetic techniques, we and others showed that orexin neurons modulate sleep/wake cycles in rodents (Adamantidis et al., 2007; Sasaki et al., 2011; Tsunematsu et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Adamantidis et al., 2007; Sasaki et al., 2011; and Tsunematsu et al., 2011.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of orexin neurons increased locomotion, feeding behavior and metabolism.
source: In addition to these, employing transgenic mice, we reported that chemogenetic activation of orexin neurons increased locomotion, feeding behavior and metabolism (Inutsuka et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Inutsuka et al., 2014.

claim: Orexin neurons contain other neurotransmitters including glutamate, dynorphin and galanin.
source: However, orexin neurons contain other neurotransmitters including glutamate (Rosin et al., 2003), dynorphin (Chou et al., 2001) and galanin (Håkansson et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rosin et al., 2003; Chou et al., 2001; and Håkansson et al., 1999.

claim: mTFP expression was observed in 80.9 ± 4.4% of orexin-immunoreactive neurons in Orexin-Flp; FSF-mTFP1 bigenic mice.
source: Immunohistochemical analysis showed mTFP expression in 80.9 ± 4.4% of orexin-immunoreactive neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical data presented in the manuscript.

claim: No ectopic expression of EGFP and/or mTFP1 protein was observed in melanin-concentrating hormone (MCH)-immunoreactive neurons in Orexin-Flp; FSF-mTFP1 bigenic mice.
source: We observed no ectopic expression of EGFP and/or mTFP1 protein in melanin-concentrating hormone (MCH)-immunoreactive (n = 4 mice; Figure 1C and D) or in any other non-orexin-immunoreactive neurons in these bigenic mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical data and Figure 1C and D.

claim: All reporter gene-expressing neurons were orexin-immunoreactive in Orexin-Flp; FSF-mTFP1 bigenic mice.
source: In other words, all reporter gene-expressing neurons were orexin-immunoreactive (IR).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical analysis data.

claim: Functional Flp was expressed exclusively in the orexin neurons of newly generated OF mice.
source: Together, these data confirmed that functional Flp was expressed exclusively in the orexin neurons of newly generated OF mice.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the immunohistochemical data showing specificity of expression.

claim: Orexin-immunoreactivity was absent in the LHA in OF (KI/KI) homozygous mice.
source: As expected, we found that EGFP expressing neurons were distributed in the LHA, however, orexin-immunoreactivity was absent in the LHA in OF (KI/KI) homozygous mice (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In heterozygous OF (KI/-) mice, 41.1 ± 5.2% of orexin-positive neurons were colocalized with EGFP.
source: In heterozygous OF (KI/-) mice, 41.1 ± 5.2% of orexin-positive neurons were colocalized with EGFP (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative immunohistochemical data.

claim: 567 ± 25 orexin-positive and 673 ± 55 dynorphin-positive cells/animal were counted in heterozygous mice (n = 3 mice).
source: We stained every 4th slice of mouse brain containing LHA and counted 567 ± 25 orexin-positive and 673 ± 55 dynorphin-positive cells/animal in heterozygous mice (n = 3 mice).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell counting data from immunohistochemistry.

claim: 84.9 ± 4.4% of dynorphin-positive neurons co-expressed orexin in heterozygous mice.
source: Among the counted neurons, 84.9 ± 4.4% of dynorphin-positive neurons co-expressed orexin (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-expression analysis data.

claim: 661 ± 15 dynorphin-positive cells/animal were counted in homozygous mice (n = 3 mice), with no orexin-positive neurons found.
source: However, while we counted 661 ± 15 dynorphin-positive cells/animal, we did not find any orexin-positive neurons in the homozygous mice (n = 3 mice, Hetero vs Homo, p=0.847 (dynorphin), p=2.4e-5 (orexin), unpaired t-test), showing that the number of dynorphin-positive cells were comparable to that in heterozygous animals.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell counting data and statistical analysis.

claim: The number of dynorphin-positive cells were comparable between heterozygous and homozygous animals.
source: However, while we counted 661 ± 15 dynorphin-positive cells/animal, we did not find any orexin-positive neurons in the homozygous mice (n = 3 mice, Hetero vs Homo, p=0.847 (dynorphin), p=2.4e-5 (orexin), unpaired t-test), showing that the number of dynorphin-positive cells were comparable to that in heterozygous animals.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison (p=0.847) of cell counts.

claim: Orexin neurons in homozygous mice did not express orexin, however, expression of dynorphin was unaffected.
source: These immunohistochemical studies confirmed that orexin neurons in homozygous mice did not express orexin, however, expression of dynorphin was unaffected.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical data comparing orexin and dynorphin expression.

claim: Orexin neurons in OF (KI/KI) mice had significantly hyperpolarized membrane potential (−58.8 ± 1.2 mV; n = 21 cells) compared to OF (KI/-) mice (−51.6 ± 0.9 mV; n = 21 cells, p=1.0e-5) and OE mice (−50.4 ± 0.9 mV; n = 22 cells, p=3.5e-7).
source: Orexin neurons in the OF (KI/KI) mice were found to have significantly hyperpolarized membrane potential (−58.8 ± 1.2 mV; n = 21 cells) compared to OF (KI/-) mice (−51.6 ± 0.9 mV; n = 21 cells, p=1.0e-5) and OE mice (−50.4 ± 0.9 mV; n = 22 cells, p=3.5e-7; Figure 4A–i–4A-iv).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Spontaneous firing frequency was significantly lower in orexin neurons in OF (KI/KI) mice (1.5 ± 0.2 Hz; n = 25 cells) compared to OF (KI/-) mice (2.5 ± 0.3 Hz; n = 21 cells, p=0.015) and OE mice (2.6 ± 0.2 Hz; n = 25, p=0.004).
source: Spontaneous firing frequency measured by cell-attached recordings were also found to be significantly lower in orexin neurons in OF (KI/KI) mice (1.5 ± 0.2 Hz; n = 25 cells) compared to OF (KI/-) mice (2.5 ± 0.3 Hz; n = 21 cells, p=0.015) and OE mice (2.6 ± 0.2 Hz; n = 25, p=0.004; Figure 4B–i–4B-iv).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell-attached recording data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The lower discharge rate in OF (KI/KI) mice could be attributed to the hyperpolarized membrane potential of orexin neurons.
source: This lower discharge rate could be attributed to the hyperpolarized membrane potential of orexin neurons in homozygous mice.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observed correlation between hyperpolarized membrane potential and lower firing rate.

claim: Orexin neurons in OF (KI/KI) mice had significantly lower input resistance (485.9 ± 35.8 MΩ; n = 23 cells) compared to OF (KI/-) mice (639.9 ± 48.2 MΩ; n = 21 cells, p=0.037) and OE mice (638.2 ± 43.4 MΩ; n = 24 cells, p=0.032).
source: In mice lacking orexin peptide (OF (KI/KI) mice), orexin neurons were found to have significantly lower input resistance (485.9 ± 35.8 MΩ; n = 23 cells) compared to OF (KI/-) mice (639.9 ± 48.2 MΩ; n = 21 cells, p=0.037) and OE mice (638.2 ± 43.4 MΩ; n = 24 cells, p=0.032; Figure 4C–i–4C-iv).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The lower input resistance in neurons lacking orexin peptides suggests that greater synaptic inputs (current injection) are necessary to generate changes in membrane potential.
source: The lower input resistance in neurons lacking orexin peptides suggests that greater synaptic inputs (current injection) are necessary to generate changes in membrane potential.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the relationship between input resistance and membrane potential changes.

claim: Orexin neurons in OF (KI/KI) mice had significantly higher membrane capacitance (35.4 ± 1.3 pF; n = 25 cells) than OF (KI/-) mice (29.9 ± 1.5 pF; n = 25 cells, p=0.012) and OE mice (30.0 ± 1.3 pF; n = 25 cells, p=0.014).
source: Interestingly, we observed that orexin neurons in OF (KI/KI) mice had significantly higher membrane capacitance (35.4 ± 1.3 pF; n = 25 cells) than OF (KI/-) mice (29.9 ± 1.5 pF; n = 25 cells, p=0.012) and OE mice (30.0 ± 1.3 pF; n = 25 cells, p=0.014, one-way ANOVA post-hoc Tukey; Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Higher capacitance in orexin neurons that lack orexin peptides reflects the increased surface area of the plasma membrane.
source: This higher capacitance in orexin neurons that lack orexin peptides reflects the increased surface area of the plasma membrane.
evidence: The claim is based on the established relationship between membrane capacitance and surface area.

claim: Orexin neuropeptide is essential for maintaining the active and passive electrophysiological properties of orexin neurons.
source: Taken together, these data clearly suggest that orexin neuropeptide is essential for maintaining the active and passive electrophysiological properties of orexin neurons.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined electrophysiological data showing altered properties in orexin-lacking neurons.

claim: Orexin neurons lacking orexin protein had significantly lower sEPSC frequency while the amplitudes were unaffected.
source: We found that orexin neurons lacking orexin protein had significantly lower sEPSC frequency while the amplitudes were unaffected (Figure 5A–5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by voltage clamp recording data shown in Figure 5A-5E.

claim: The average inter-event interval for all recorded sEPSCs of orexin neurons in OF (KI/KI) mice was 247.2 ± 48.6 ms (n = 29 cells) while that of OF (KI/-) mice was 116.7 ± 7.6 ms (n = 25 cells, p=0.01 vs OF (KI/KI)) and OE mice was 77.9 ± 7.4 ms (n = 26 cells, p=5.8e-4 vs OF (KI/KI)).
source: The average inter-event interval for all recorded sEPSCs of orexin neurons in OF (KI/KI) mice was 247.2 ± 48.6 ms (n = 29 cells) while that of OF (KI/-) mice was 116.7 ± 7.6 ms (n = 25 cells, p=0.01 vs OF (KI/KI)) and OE mice was 77.9 ± 7.4 ms (n = 26 cells, p=5.8e-4 vs OF (KI/KI), one-way ANOVA pot-hoc Tukey; Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by sEPSC recording data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The sEPSC amplitude of orexin neurons in OF (KI/KI) mice was 22.6 ± 1.3 pA (n = 29 cells) while that of OF (KI/-) mice was 22.6 ± 1.3 pA (n = 25 cells, p=1.0 OF (KI/KI)) and in OE mice was 20.5 ± 1.1 pA (n = 26 cells, p=0.46 vs OF (KI/KI)).
source: The sEPSC amplitude of orexin neurons in OF (KI/KI) mice was 22.6 ± 1.3 pA (n = 29 cells) while that of OF (KI/-) mice was 22.6 ± 1.3 pA (n = 25 cells, p=1.0 OF (KI/KI)) and in OE mice was 20.5 ± 1.1 pA (n = 26 cells, p=0.46 vs OF (KI/KI), one-way ANOVA post-hoc Tukey; Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by sEPSC amplitude measurements and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: sIPSCs in neurons lacking orexin peptides showed a tendency toward decreasing frequency and amplitude, but these changes were not statistically significant.
source: Although sIPSCs in neurons lacking orexin peptides showed a tendency toward decreasing frequency and amplitude, these changes were not statistically significant.
evidence: The claim is supported by sIPSC recording data showing trends without statistical significance.

claim: The inter-event interval for sIPSCs in orexin neurons in OF (KI/KI) mice was 835.0 ± 124.6 ms (n = 17 cells) while that of OF (KI/-) mice was 642.4 ± 70.9 ms (n = 22 cells, p=0.35 vs OF (KI/KI)) and in OE mice was 595.0 ± 96.7 ms (n = 21 cells, p=0.21 vs OF (KI/KI)).
source: The inter-event interval for sIPSCs in orexin neurons in OF (KI/KI) mice was 835.0 ± 124.6 ms (n = 17 cells) while that of OF (KI/-) mice was 642.4 ± 70.9 ms (n = 22 cells, p=0.35 vs OF (KI/KI)) and in OE mice was 595.0 ± 96.7 ms (n = 21 cells, p=0.21 vs OF (KI/KI), one-way ANOVA post-hoc Tukey; Figure 5H).
evidence: The claim is supported by sIPSC recording data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The sIPSC amplitude in orexin neurons in OF (KI/KI) mice was 48.4 ± 6.1 pA (n = 17 cells) while that of OF (KI/-) mice was 52.5 ± 3.9 pA (n = 22 cells, p=0.86 vs OF (KI/KI)) and in OE mice was 57.7 ± 6.5 pA (n = 21 cells, p=0.48 vs OF (KI/KI)).
source: The sIPSC amplitude in orexin neurons in OF (KI/KI) mice was 48.4 ± 6.1 pA (n = 17 cells) while that of OF (KI/-) mice was 52.5 ± 3.9 pA (n = 22 cells, p=0.86 vs OF (KI/KI)) and in OE mice was 57.7 ± 6.5 pA (n = 21 cells, p=0.48 vs OF (KI/KI), one-way ANOVA post-hoc Tukey; Figure 5I).
evidence: The claim is supported by sIPSC amplitude measurements and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Orexin plays a role in maintaining the physiological input-output functions in orexin neurons.
source: These, along with previous, results indicate that orexin plays a role in maintaining the physiological input-output functions in orexin neurons.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined synaptic input data showing altered glutamatergic inputs in orexin-lacking neurons.

claim: All recorded OF (KI/KI) mice showed cataplexy attack, especially during the start of the dark period.
source: All recorded OF (KI/KI) mice showed cataplexy attack, especially during the start of the dark period.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral recording data from sleep/wakefulness analysis.

claim: OF (KI/KI) mice showed less wakefulness and higher NREM and REM sleep compared to the WT control animals.
source: As expected, OF (KI/KI) mice showed less wakefulness and higher NREM and REM sleep compared to the WT control animals (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by vigilance state data presented in Table 1.

claim: Orexin KO mice showed an increased number of bouts and decreased average duration in all vigilance states, suggesting fragmentation of the sleep-wakefulness and an inability to maintain sustained arousal in the absence of orexin peptides.
source: Along with these changes, orexin KO mice showed an increased number of bouts and decreased average duration in all vigilance states (Table 1), suggesting fragmentation of the sleep-wakefulness and an inability to maintain sustained arousal in the absence of orexin peptides.
evidence: The claim is supported by vigilance state data in Table 1 and inference about the functional consequences.

claim: 92.1 ± 0.6% of orexin-immunoreactive cells expressed mCherry in heterozygous mice (n = 3 mice).
source: The number of orexin-immunoreactive cells was 439 ± 23 cells/mouse in the brain of heterozygous mice and, among these, 92.1 ± 0.6% expressed mCherry (n = 3 mice; Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: A very similar number of LHA neurons expressed mCherry in both heterozygous and homozygous mice: 422 ± 80 cells/animal (n = 6 mice) in OF (KI/-) and 455 ± 74 cells/animal (n = 6 mice) in OF (KI/KI) mice (p=0.76).
source: Moreover, a very similar number of LHA neurons expressed mCherry in both heterozygous and homozygous mice: 422 ± 80 cells/animal (n = 6 mice) in OF (KI/-) and 455 ± 74 cells/animal (n = 6 mice) in OF (KI/KI) mice expressed mCherry (p=0.76, unpaired t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell counting data and statistical comparison.

claim: In heterozygous mice, the ratio of c-Fos expression in mCherry-positive cells of saline or CNO injected mice was 11.6 ± 1.9% or 89.2 ± 1.4%, respectively (n = 3 mice/group, p=9.2e-5).
source: In heterozygous mice, the ratio of c-Fos expression in mCherry-positive cells of saline or CNO injected mice was 11.6 ± 1.9% or 89.2 ± 1.4%, respectively (n = 3 mice/group, p=9.2e-5, Figure 6C–6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by c-Fos immunostaining data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 6C-6D.

claim: In homozygous mice, the ratio of c-Fos expression in mCherry-positive cells of saline or CNO injected mice was 10.6 ± 1.8% or 90.3 ± 1.1%, respectively (n = 3 mice/group, p=9.6e-4).
source: In homozygous mice, the ratio of c-Fos expression in mCherry-positive cells of saline or CNO injected mice was 10.6 ± 1.8% or 90.3 ± 1.1%, respectively (n = 3 mice/group, p=9.6e-4, paired t-test, Figure 6C–6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by c-Fos immunostaining data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 6C-6D.

claim: The DREADD system successfully enabled selective activation of orexin neurons in both heterozygous and homozygous mice.
source: Thus, we concluded that the DREADD system successfully enabled selective activation of orexin neurons in both heterozygous and homozygous mice.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the c-Fos expression data showing CNO-induced activation.

claim: In OF (KI/-) mice, activation of orexin neurons increased total time spent in wakefulness and decreased time in REM sleep and in NREM sleep after CNO administration during both the light and dark periods.
source: Expectedly in OF (KI/-) mice, activation of orexin neurons increased total time spent in wakefulness (n = 9 mice, Figures 7B–I and 8D–I) and decreased time in REM sleep (Figure 7B–ii and D-ii) and in NREM sleep (Figure 7B–iii and D-iii) after CNO administration during both the light and dark periods (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by sleep/wake recording data shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: The effects of orexin neuronal activation in OF (KI/KI) mice were comparable to the OF (KI/-) control during the dark period, but were dampened during the light period.
source: However, while the effects of orexin neuronal activation in OF (KI/KI) mice were comparable to the OF (KI/-) control during the dark period, it was dampened during the light period (n = 8 mice, Wakefulness: Figure 7B–i and D–I; REM sleep: Figure 7B–ii and D-ii; and NREM sleep: Figure 7B–iii and B-iii, and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by sleep/wake recording data comparing light and dark periods shown in Figure 7.

claim: Co-transmitters could partially compensate for the increased wakefulness in the absence of orexin.
source: This clear difference could be explained by the ability of co-transmitters to partially compensate for the increased wakefulness.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that OF (KI/KI) mice showed some wakefulness increase despite lacking orexin.

claim: Activation of orexin neurons that lacked orexin peptide deteriorated cataplexy during the light periods (saline (L): 0.2 ± 0.1 min/hr; CNO (L): 0.9 ± 0.3 min/hr, n = 8 mice, p=0.04).
source: Surprisingly, however, activation of orexin neurons that lacked orexin peptide rather deteriorate the cataplexy during the light periods while it showed similar propensity during the dark period (saline (L): 0.2 ± 0.1 min/hr; CNO (L): 0.9 ± 0.3 min/hr, n = 8 mice, p=0.04; saline (D): 3.0 ± 1.2 min/hr; CNO (D): 5.2 ± 1.4 min/hr, n = 8 mice, p=0.14; Figure 7B-iv and 7D-iv).
evidence: The claim is supported by cataplexy recording data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 7B-iv and 7D-iv.

claim: Activation of orexin neurons showed similar cataplexy propensity during the dark period (saline (D): 3.0 ± 1.2 min/hr; CNO (D): 5.2 ± 1.4 min/hr, n = 8 mice, p=0.14).
source: Surprisingly, however, activation of orexin neurons that lacked orexin peptide rather deteriorate the cataplexy during the light periods while it showed similar propensity during the dark period (saline (L): 0.2 ± 0.1 min/hr; CNO (L): 0.9 ± 0.3 min/hr, n = 8 mice, p=0.04; saline (D): 3.0 ± 1.2 min/hr; CNO (D): 5.2 ± 1.4 min/hr, n = 8 mice, p=0.14; Figure 7B-iv and 7D-iv).
evidence: The claim is supported by cataplexy recording data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 7B-iv and 7D-iv.

claim: CNO itself has no effect on the initiation or maintenance of cataplectic attack in the Prepro-orexin KO (OXKO) mice.
source: CNO itself is reported to have no effect on the initiation or maintenance of cataplectic attack in the Prepro-orexin KO (OXKO) mice (Mahoney et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Mahoney et al., 2017.

claim: Neurotransmitters other than orexin could partially compensate for abnormalities in the regulation of sleep/wakefulness, excluding cataplexy.
source: These results clearly suggested that neurotransmitters other than orexin could partially compensate for abnormalities in the regulation of sleep/wakefulness, excluding cataplexy.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined behavioral data showing differential effects on wakefulness versus cataplexy.

claim: In OF (KI/-) mice, total observed bouts decreased in all three vigilance states for 2 hr after CNO injection.
source: Whereas, in OF (KI/-) mice, total observed bouts decrease in all three vigilance states for 2 hr after CNO injection (Wakefulness: Figure 7C–i and E–i; REM: Figure 7C–ii and E-ii, NREM: Figure 7C–iii and 7E-iii), they remain unaffected in case of OF (KI/KI) mice (Wakefulness: Figure 7C–i and E–i; REM: Figure 7C–ii and 7E-ii, NREM: Figure 7C–iii and 7E-iii; Cataplexy: Figure 7C-iv and 7E-iv).
evidence: The claim is supported by bout analysis data shown in Figure 7C and 7E.

claim: Total observed bouts remained unaffected in OF (KI/KI) mice after CNO injection.
source: Whereas, in OF (KI/-) mice, total observed bouts decrease in all three vigilance states for 2 hr after CNO injection (Wakefulness: Figure 7C–i and E–i; REM: Figure 7C–ii and E-ii, NREM: Figure 7C–iii and 7E-iii), they remain unaffected in case of OF (KI/KI) mice (Wakefulness: Figure 7C–i and E–i; REM: Figure 7C–ii and 7E-ii, NREM: Figure 7C–iii and 7E-iii; Cataplexy: Figure 7C-iv and 7E-iv).
evidence: The claim is supported by bout analysis data shown in Figure 7C and 7E.

claim: Orexin neuronal activation increased average wake duration in OF (KI/-) mice and decreased REM sleep and NREM sleep duration.
source: Conversely, orexin neuronal activation increased average wake duration in OF (KI/-) mice (Figure 7C–i and E–i); and decreased REM sleep (Figure 7C–ii and 7E-ii) and NREM sleep duration (Figure 7C–iii and 7E-iii).
evidence: The claim is supported by duration analysis data shown in Figure 7C and 7E.

claim: In OF (KI/KI) mice, while the total wake time was increased after chemogenetic activation, duration of wake was not extended.
source: However, in case of OF (KI/KI) mice, while the total wake time was increased after chemogenetic activation (Figure 7B and 7E i-iv), duration of wake was not extended (Wakefulness: Figure 7C–i and E–i; REM: Figure 7C–ii and 7E-ii; NREM: Figure 7C–iii and 7E-iii; Cataplexy: Figure 7C-iv and 7E-iv).
evidence: The claim is supported by wake time and duration analysis data shown in Figure 7B, 7C, and 7E.

claim: Orexin neuropeptide was indispensable to promote sustained arousal, where the co-transmitters could not compensate.
source: Together, all these experimental analyses indicated that orexin neuropeptide was indispensable to promote sustained arousal, where the co-transmitters could not compensate.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined behavioral data showing that wake duration was not extended in OF (KI/KI) mice.

claim: CNO-induced cataplexy showed similar electrocortical activity as the naïve cataplexy attack observed in OF (KI/-) mice.
source: Relative power analysis showed no difference in either power of the delta, theta, alpha or beta wave (n = 8 mice, Figure 8C), suggesting that CNO-induced cataplexy showed similar electrocortical activity as the naïve cataplexy attack observed in OF (KI/-) mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by EEG power spectrum analysis data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Orexin is essential to maintain basic membrane properties and input-output computation of orexin neurons.
source: Taken together, orexin is essential to maintain basic membrane properties and input-output computation of orexin neurons, as well as to exert awake-sustaining aptitude of orexin neurons.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by the combined electrophysiological and behavioral data.

claim: Orexin is essential to exert awake-sustaining aptitude of orexin neurons.
source: Taken together, orexin is essential to maintain basic membrane properties and input-output computation of orexin neurons, as well as to exert awake-sustaining aptitude of orexin neurons.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by the behavioral data showing inability to maintain sustained arousal without orexin.

claim: Both orexin and co-transmitters functioned to increase wakefulness.
source: Selective chemogenetic activation revealed that both orexin and co-transmitters functioned to increase wakefulness, however, orexin was indispensable to promote sustained arousal.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by the chemogenetic activation data.

claim: Orexin was indispensable to promote sustained arousal.
source: Selective chemogenetic activation revealed that both orexin and co-transmitters functioned to increase wakefulness, however, orexin was indispensable to promote sustained arousal.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by the wake duration data.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of orexin neurons without orexin increased the total time spent in cataplexy.
source: Surprisingly, such activation increased the total time spent in cataplexy.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by the cataplexy recording data.

claim: Orexin neurons without orexin showed altered electrophysiological properties.
source: Orexin neurons without orexin showed altered electrophysiological properties, as well as received decreased glutamatergic inputs.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by the electrophysiological recording data.

claim: Orexin neurons without orexin received decreased glutamatergic inputs.
source: Orexin neurons without orexin showed altered electrophysiological properties, as well as received decreased glutamatergic inputs.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by the sEPSC recording data.

claim: Orexin neuropeptide depolarized orexin neurons via OX2R and mediates a positive-feedback loop both directly and indirectly.
source: Previously, we reported that orexin neuropeptide depolarized orexin neurons via OX2R and mediates a positive-feedback loop both directly and indirectly (Yamanaka et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Yamanaka et al., 2010.

claim: Orexin facilitates glutamate release onto orexin neurons.
source: In agreement with this, we also found that orexin facilitates glutamate release onto orexin neurons.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the decreased glutamatergic inputs observed in orexin-lacking neurons.

claim: An approximately 3 pF increase in capacitance is estimated to be associated with a 1–2 µm increase in diameter as a spherical body.
source: We did not directly measure the difference in diameter of cell size since an approximately 3 pF increase is estimated to be associated with a 1–2 µm increase in diameter as a spherical body.
evidence: The claim is based on established biophysical relationships between capacitance and cell size.

claim: Orexin A and B are expressed at 1 week of age during early postnatal brain development.
source: Satoyanova et al. showed that orexin A and B are expressed at 1 week of age during early postnatal brain development (Stoyanova et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Stoyanova et al., 2010.

claim: Orexin increased the temporal synchrony of action potentials in developing locus coeruleus cells.
source: In addition to this, van den Pol et al. showed that orexin increased the temporal synchrony of action potentials in developing locus coeruleus cells (van den Pol et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to van den Pol et al., 2002.

claim: Orexin might have a role in brain development.
source: These reports suggest that orexin might have a role in brain development.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the cited studies showing orexin expression and effects during development.

claim: Human narcolepsy patients show chronic daytime sleepiness.
source: Orexin neurons are known to play an essential role in maintaining uninterrupted wakefulness as human narcolepsy patients show chronic daytime sleepiness (Crocker et al., 2005; Thannickal et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Crocker et al., 2005 and Thannickal et al., 2000.

claim: Disruption of orexin signaling in mice, rats and dogs produces a phenotype which includes short bouts of wakefulness and increased transitions of vigilance states.
source: Disruption of orexin signaling in mice, rats and dogs produce a very similar phenotype which includes short bouts of wakefulness and increased transitions of vigilance states (Chemelli et al., 1999; Mochizuki et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chemelli et al., 1999 and Mochizuki et al., 2004.

claim: Orexin administration can make wakefulness with high cognitive ability in non-human primates.
source: Moreover, orexin administration can also make wakefulness with high cognitive ability in non-human primates (Deadwyler et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Deadwyler et al., 2007.

claim: The level of orexin peptide in the CSF is low during the light period and high during the active-wake period in rodents.
source: In rodents, the level of orexin peptide in the CSF is low during the light period and high during the active-wake period (Zeitzer et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Zeitzer et al., 2003.

claim: Orexin neurons show higher activity during active wakefulness and become less active or inactive during REM or NREM sleep.
source: Moreover, orexin neurons supposedly show higher activity during active wakefulness and become less active or inactive during REM or NREM sleep (Lee et al., 2005; Mileykovskiy et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lee et al., 2005 and Mileykovskiy et al., 2005.

claim: The activity of orexin neurons is differentially regulated during the light and dark periods.
source: Our data also suggest that the activity of orexin neurons is differentially regulated during the light and dark periods.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the differential effects of CNO observed during light versus dark periods.

claim: The higher endogenous activity of orexin neurons during the dark period may facilitate CNO-induced transmitter release resulting in improved wakefulness in OF(KI/KI) mice.
source: It is possible that the higher endogenous activity of orexin neurons during the dark period may facilitate CNO-induced transmitter release resulting in improved wakefulness in OF(KI/KI) mice.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about the mechanism underlying the observed differential effects.

claim: The primary function of orexin is to maintain the electrophysiological balance, the input-output functions in orexin neurons and to exert the function of orexin neurons in maintaining sustained wakefulness.
source: In summary, here we dissociated the role of orexin at the cellular and behavioral level. We suggest that the primary function of orexin is to maintain the electrophysiological balance, the input-output functions in orexin neurons and most importantly, to exert the function of orexin neurons in maintaining sustained wakefulness.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion inferred from all the experimental data presented.

claim: Orexin content was decreased to 75% in heterozygous mice.
source: Chemelli et al. reported that orexin A content was decreased to 75% in heterozygous mice. (Chemelli et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Chemelli et al., 1999.

claim: OF (KI/-) mice showed a shorter duration of wakefulness compared with WT control mice, likely due to the decrease in orexin.
source: OF (KI/-) mice showed a shorter duration of wakefulness compared with WT control mice, and is likely due to the decrease in orexin.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed phenotype and the known decrease in orexin content in heterozygous mice.

claim: GABAergic neurons in the ventral tegmental area inhibited orexin neuronal activity by making monosynaptic inhibitory projections and regulate NREM sleep in mice.
source: By using the Orexin-Flp; Gad67-Cre bigenic mice, we recently found that GABAergic neurons in the ventral tegmental area inhibited orexin neuronal activity by making monosynaptic inhibitory projections and regulate NERM sleep in mice (Chowdhury et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Chowdhury et al., 2019.

claim: Serotonergic neurons in the raphe nucleus inhibit orexin neurons both directly and indirectly.
source: Recently, we reported that serotonergic neurons in the raphe nucleus inhibit orexin neurons both directly and indirectly (Chowdhury and Yamanaka, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Chowdhury and Yamanaka, 2016.

claim: Orexin neurons form a positive-feedback circuitry among themselves in the LHA by activating other orexin neurons through OX2R.
source: Most interestingly, orexin neurons form a positive-feedback circuitry among themselves in the LHA by activating other orexin neurons through OX2R to maintain the wake-active network at optimum level and/or for a sustained period (Yamanaka et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Yamanaka et al., 2010.

claim: Intracerebroventricular injection of orexin inhibited cataplexy.
source: It is also possible that the released orexin diffuses in the CSF since intracerebroventricular injection of orexin inhibited cataplexy (Mieda et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Mieda et al., 2004.

claim: Orexin co-transmitter dynorphin inhibits orexin neurons both directly and indirectly by depressing glutamatergic afferent inputs to orexin neurons.
source: Moreover, orexin co-transmitter dynorphin, which inhibits orexin neurons both directly and indirectly by depressing glutamatergic afferent inputs to orexin neurons, might also play a key role in such deterioration of cataplexy (Li and van den Pol, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Li and van den Pol, 2006.

claim: The release of orexin follows a circadian rhythm that is also strongly related to locomotion.
source: The release of orexin follows a circadian rhythm that is also strongly related to locomotion (Zhang et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2004.
